questions.question: The tribal festival 'Hal Punhya' is traditionally associated with which of the following states?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jharkhand**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Hal Punhya** is a traditional tribal festival celebrated in the state of **Jharkhand**.
 
• This festival marks the **beginning of the agricultural season** and is observed with great enthusiasm by the tribal communities.
 
• The festival is celebrated by **ploughing the land for the first time** in the agricultural season, symbolizing the start of farming activities.
 
• It is mainly celebrated by tribes such as the **Munda, Oraon, and Santhal** communities, which are prominent tribal groups in Jharkhand.
 
• During the festival, prayers are offered to the **local deities** and spirits to seek blessings for a bountiful harvest.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tribal Festivals of Jharkhand:**

 
 
• Jharkhand, known as the **"Land of Forests"**, is home to a significant tribal population that celebrates a variety of festivals rooted in their traditions and agricultural practices.
 
• Other major tribal festivals include **Sarhul** (worship of Sal tree), **Karma** (celebration of nature), and **Jani Shikar** (hunting festival).
 
 
 
• **Importance of Tribal Festivals:**
 
 
• Tribal festivals like Hal Punhya are closely linked to **nature and agriculture**, reflecting the tribal community's respect for the environment.
 
• These festivals promote **community bonding** and serve as an opportunity for the tribes to come together and celebrate their rich cultural heritage.
 
 
 
• **Jharkhand's Agricultural Practices:**
 
 
• Agriculture is the main occupation in Jharkhand, and festivals like Hal Punhya symbolize the **beginning of the sowing season**.
 
• The state primarily grows crops like **rice, maize, pulses, and oilseeds**.
 
 
 
• **Other Tribal States in India:**
 
 
• India is home to several states with a rich tribal culture, including **Madhya Pradesh**, **Chhattisgarh**, **Odisha**, and **Rajasthan**.
 
• Each state has its unique tribal festivals and traditions that are deeply rooted in their lifestyle and environment.

questions.question: Which of the following is responsible for emulsification of fats?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bile**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Bile** is a digestive fluid produced by the **liver** and stored in the **gallbladder**.
 
• It plays a crucial role in the digestion and absorption of fats by breaking large fat globules into smaller droplets, a process called **emulsification**.
 
• Emulsification of fats increases the surface area for the enzyme **lipase** to act upon, leading to more efficient fat digestion.
 
• Bile contains **bile salts**, which are amphipathic molecules (having both hydrophilic and hydrophobic parts) that help in the emulsification process.
 
• In addition to bile salts, bile also contains **cholesterol, phospholipids, and waste products** like bilirubin, which are excreted from the body.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Other Digestive Enzymes and Substances:**

 
 
• **Rennin:** An enzyme found in the stomach of young mammals, it helps in the digestion of milk by converting casein (milk protein) into a curd-like substance. It is not involved in fat digestion.
 
• **Pepsin:** A digestive enzyme secreted by the stomach, it breaks down proteins into smaller peptides. It does not play a role in emulsifying fats.
 
• **Lipase:** A pancreatic enzyme that breaks down triglycerides (fats) into glycerol and free fatty acids. However, lipase requires emulsified fats for effective action, which is facilitated by bile.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Emulsification:**
 
 
• Emulsification is essential for the proper digestion and absorption of dietary fats.
 
• The smaller fat droplets formed during emulsification can mix more easily with water, facilitating the action of lipase.
 
• This process also ensures that essential nutrients like fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are absorbed efficiently in the intestines.
 
 
 
• **Bile Production and Storage:**
 
 
• The **liver** produces about 800–1,000 mL of bile daily.
 
• The produced bile is stored in the **gallbladder** and released into the small intestine (duodenum) when fatty food is consumed.
 
 
 
• **Gallbladder Disorders:**
 
 
• Issues like **gallstones** can obstruct bile flow, leading to improper fat digestion and related symptoms such as bloating and fatty stools.
 
• The removal of the gallbladder (cholecystectomy) does not stop bile production but affects the storage and regulated release of bile.

questions.question: In which of the following years did the construction of the Gateway of India in Mumbai begin?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**In 1911**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The construction of the **Gateway of India** in Mumbai began in the year **1911**.
 
• This iconic monument was built to commemorate the visit of **King George V and Queen Mary** to India during the **Delhi Durbar** in December 1911.
 
• The foundation stone of the Gateway of India was laid on **31 March 1911**, although the construction officially started later.
 
• The design of the Gateway was prepared by architect **George Wittet**, combining **Indo-Saracenic architecture** with elements of **Islamic** and **Hindu architectural styles**.
 
• The final construction of the Gateway of India was completed in **1924**, and it officially opened to the public the same year.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Historical Context:**

 
 
• The Gateway of India was built to honor the arrival of **British royals King George V and Queen Mary** to India for the first time in 1911.
 
• The monument symbolizes **British colonial rule** in India and was intended to serve as the ceremonial entry point to the country.
 
• It became a symbol of the British Empire's grandeur during its reign in India.
 
 
 
• **Architectural Features:**
 
 
• The Gateway of India is designed in the **Indo-Saracenic style**, which blends **Hindu** and **Muslim architectural elements**, a popular style during British rule in India.
 
• The structure is made of **yellow basalt** and reinforced concrete, giving it a robust and majestic appearance.
 
• It stands at a height of approximately **26 meters (85 feet)** and features intricate stone latticework and decorative motifs.
 
 
 
• **Significance:**
 
 
• The Gateway of India later became an important historical landmark, marking the departure of the last British troops from India in **1948**, following India's independence in 1947.
 
• It is now a **major tourist attraction** and serves as a symbolic reminder of the colonial era.
 
 
 
• **Other Events:**
 
 
• The Gateway of India overlooks the **Arabian Sea** and is located at the Apollo Bunder area in South Mumbai.
 
• It is near other historical landmarks, such as the **Taj Mahal Palace Hotel**, enhancing its cultural significance.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Milestones in Construction:**

 
 
• The foundation stone was laid in **1911**, but the construction was delayed and officially started in **1913**.
 
• The monument was inaugurated on **4 December 1924**, by the then Viceroy of India, **Rufus Isaacs, Lord Reading**.
 
 
 
• **Relevance Today:**
 
 
• The Gateway of India serves as a venue for cultural events, national celebrations, and public gatherings in Mumbai.
 
• It is a popular spot for photography and a starting point for ferries to **Elephanta Caves**, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: The book 'Beyond Religion: Ethics for a Whole World' has been written by whom?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dalai Lama**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Dalai Lama**, the spiritual leader of Tibet, authored the book **'Beyond Religion: Ethics for a Whole World'**, which was published in **2011**.
 
• The book emphasizes the importance of **secular ethics** that transcend religion, advocating compassion, understanding, and mutual respect as universal values.
 
• It provides a framework for addressing global challenges by focusing on human values and ethical principles rather than religious ideologies.
 
• The Dalai Lama's teachings in the book aim to promote peace, sustainability, and harmony in a diverse and interconnected world.
 
• This work reflects the Dalai Lama's lifelong commitment to **nonviolence**, **interfaith dialogue**, and fostering universal responsibility among humanity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Dalai Lama:**

 
 
• The Dalai Lama is the **spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism** and a global advocate for peace and compassion.
 
• Born as **Tenzin Gyatso** in **1935**, he is the 14th Dalai Lama and has lived in **exile in India** since **1959** after fleeing Tibet due to Chinese occupation.
 
• The Dalai Lama has authored numerous books addressing **philosophy, ethics, and spirituality**, including **'The Art of Happiness'** and **'Ancient Wisdom, Modern World'**.
 
• He was awarded the **Nobel Peace Prize** in **1989** for his efforts to promote peaceful solutions to the Tibetan conflict and his commitment to nonviolence.
 
 
 
• **Other Authors Mentioned:**
 
 
• **Swami Gyanvatsal:** A spiritual leader associated with the **BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha**, known for his motivational speeches focusing on personal and professional growth.
 
• **Devdutt Pattanaik:** An Indian author and mythologist who has written extensively on Indian mythology, including books like **'Jaya'** and **'My Gita'**.
 
• **Sadhguru:** A contemporary Indian yogi and founder of the **Isha Foundation**, widely recognized for his teachings on yoga, spirituality, and personal well-being. Some of his notable works include **'Inner Engineering'**.
 
 
 
• **Key Themes of 'Beyond Religion':**
 
 
• The book advocates **secular ethics**, emphasizing the importance of values like compassion, kindness, and respect in addressing global issues.
 
• It suggests that ethical behavior can be achieved without reliance on religious doctrines, making it universally applicable across cultures and beliefs.
 
• Dalai Lama calls for individuals to take personal responsibility for creating a **peaceful and sustainable world**.
 
 
 
• **Universal Ethics:**
 
 
• The concept of secular ethics is rooted in the idea that moral principles can transcend religious or cultural boundaries.
 
• It aims to create a common ground for people from diverse backgrounds to work collaboratively toward the betterment of society.
 
• This idea has gained prominence in global discussions on **peacebuilding**, **conflict resolution**, and **sustainability**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Dalai Lama's Global Influence:**

 
 
• The Dalai Lama is recognized as a prominent figure in promoting **interfaith dialogue**, **human rights**, and **environmental conservation**.
 
• His teachings emphasize the interconnectedness of humanity and the need for compassion in addressing global crises.
 
• He has participated in numerous international forums, inspiring leaders and individuals to adopt ethical approaches to problem-solving.
 
 
 
• **Ethics in Modern Society:**
 
 
• The concept of secular ethics aligns with contemporary movements to address **climate change**, **social justice**, and **global health**.
 
• It underscores the importance of collective action and shared values in overcoming challenges faced by humanity today.

questions.question: The dynasties named Sharabhpuriya and Somvanshi ruled in ____________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chhattisgarh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Sharabhpuriya dynasty** was a ruling dynasty that flourished in the region of present-day **Chhattisgarh** during the 5th and 6th centuries CE. They were known for their patronage of religion and culture.
 
• The **Somvanshi dynasty** succeeded the Sharabhpuriya dynasty in the same region and ruled during the **7th to 8th centuries CE**. They played a significant role in the development of art and architecture in this area.
 
• Both dynasties contributed to the cultural and historical heritage of **Chhattisgarh**, which was then part of the Dakshina Kosala region.
 
• The region of Chhattisgarh, during the rule of these dynasties, saw a flourishing of **Hindu religious practices** and the construction of temples and other architectural marvels.
 
• Chhattisgarh has a rich history of dynastic rule, and these dynasties laid the foundation for many traditions and cultural practices still observed in the region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sharabhpuriya Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Sharabhpuriya dynasty is considered one of the earliest known dynasties in the region of present-day Chhattisgarh.
 
• They ruled during the **5th and 6th centuries CE** and were responsible for the early development of this region's socio-political structure.
 
• The dynasty is known for promoting **Shaivism** and constructing temples dedicated to Lord Shiva.
 
• Although there is limited historical evidence, inscriptions and local traditions provide insights into their rule.
 
 
 
• **Somvanshi Dynasty:**
 
 
• The Somvanshi dynasty succeeded the Sharabhpuriyas and ruled during the **7th to 8th centuries CE**.
 
• They were known for their administrative efficiency and contributions to art and culture.
 
• Several temples built during their reign reflect the influence of **Hindu architectural styles**.
 
• The Somvanshi rulers were patrons of religion and literature, further enriching the cultural landscape of Chhattisgarh.
 
 
 
• **Chhattisgarh Region:**
 
 
• Chhattisgarh was historically known as **Dakshina Kosala** and has a rich heritage of dynastic rule and cultural advancements.
 
• The region has been a center for **Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism**, with significant archaeological sites and monuments.
 
• It is home to various tribes and communities that have preserved ancient traditions and cultural practices.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The region of Chhattisgarh played a crucial role in ancient Indian history due to its strategic location and cultural contributions.
 
• The dynasties like Sharabhpuriya and Somvanshi contributed to the development of administrative systems and cultural practices.
 
• The transition from one dynasty to another marks the evolution of socio-political structures in the region.

questions.question: Which of the following Harappan sites is located in Gujarat?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Surkotada**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Surkotada** is a significant **Harappan site located in Gujarat**, India.
 
• This site was discovered in **1964** by **J.P. Joshi** of the Archaeological Survey of India.
 
• Surkotada is known for its unique fortification, and it provides evidence of the Harappan civilization's expansion into the Gujarat region.
 
• The site is notable for the discovery of horse remains, which are rarely found in other Harappan sites.
 
• Surkotada had a small fortified settlement with mud-brick structures, indicating urban planning and architectural proficiency.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sokhta Koh:**

 
 
• Sokhta Koh is located in **Baluchistan, Pakistan**, near the Makran coast.
 
• It is believed to have served as a trading post for Harappans, facilitating maritime trade.
 
• The site is known for its connection to the Harappan civilization's coastal trade network.
 
 
 
• **Shortugai:**
 
 
• Shortugai is located in **Afghanistan**, near the Amu Darya river.
 
• This site was a significant trading center for Harappans, particularly for importing lapis lazuli.
 
• It provides evidence of Harappan influence beyond the Indian subcontinent.
 
 
 
• **Sutkagendor:**
 
 
• Sutkagendor is situated in the **Baluchistan province of Pakistan**, near the Iranian border.
 
• The site is believed to have functioned as a coastal trade post for the Harappan civilization.
 
• Sutkagendor connects the Harappan civilization to its maritime trade networks.
 
 
 
• **Harappan Civilization:**
 
 
• The Harappan civilization, also known as the **Indus Valley Civilization**, thrived between **2600 BCE to 1900 BCE**.
 
• It was characterized by urban planning, advanced architecture, and trade networks.
 
• Major sites include **Harappa, Mohenjo-Daro, Lothal, Kalibangan, and Dholavira**.
 
• It is one of the world's earliest urban civilizations, alongside Mesopotamia and Egypt.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Surkotada's Importance:**

 
 
• Surkotada provides evidence of Harappan civilization's **geographical spread** into Gujarat.
 
• The discovery of **horse remains** at Surkotada is significant, as horses are rarely found at Harappan sites.
 
• The site demonstrates the Harappan civilization's adaptability in different geographical and ecological conditions.
 
 
 
• **Harappan Sites in Gujarat:**
 
 
• Prominent Harappan sites in Gujarat include **Lothal, Dholavira, Rangpur, and Surkotada**.
 
• These sites highlight the influence of the Harappan civilization in western India.
 
• They are known for their unique features like dockyards (Lothal), water reservoirs (Dholavira), and fortified settlements (Surkotada).

questions.question: According to Megasthenes, during the reign of Chandragupta Maurya, the society was divided into ________________ castes.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**7**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to the ancient Greek ambassador **Megasthenes**, who visited India during the reign of **Chandragupta Maurya**, Indian society was divided into **7 distinct castes or classes**.
 
• Megasthenes described these classes in his work **Indica**, which provides valuable insights into the social structure of ancient India.
 
• The seven castes included **philosophers (Brahmins), farmers, soldiers, herdsmen, artisans, magistrates, and councilors**.
 
• Each caste had its own specific roles and responsibilities in society, and these roles were strictly adhered to during the Mauryan period.
 
• This classification by Megasthenes is unique and reflects the functional division of labor in the Mauryan society, rather than the traditional caste system based on birth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Megasthenes and His Work Indica:**

 
 
• **Megasthenes** was a Greek ambassador sent by Seleucus I to the court of Chandragupta Maurya, around **302 BCE**.
 
• His book **Indica** provides one of the earliest accounts of Indian society, culture, and governance.
 
• Although the original text of Indica is lost, its content is known through later writers such as **Strabo, Arrian, and Diodorus**.
 
• Megasthenes observed and recorded various aspects of Indian civilization, including the caste system, governance, and economy.
 
 
 
• **The Seven Classes Described by Megasthenes:**
 
 
• **Philosophers:** These were scholars, priests, and teachers (likely Brahmins) engaged in spiritual and intellectual pursuits.
 
• **Farmers:** Representing the majority of the population, they were responsible for agriculture and food production.
 
• **Soldiers:** They served in the military and were tasked with the defense of the state.
 
• **Herdsmen:** They raised livestock such as cattle and were crucial to the agrarian economy.
 
• **Artisans:** This class included craftsmen and workers who produced goods and tools.
 
• **Magistrates:** They were involved in the administration of justice and governance.
 
• **Councilors:** Advisors and officials who assisted the king in decision-making and governance.
 
 
 
• **Chandragupta Maurya and the Mauryan Empire:**
 
 
• **Chandragupta Maurya** was the founder of the Mauryan Empire, which was established around **321 BCE**.
 
• He is known for unifying most of the Indian subcontinent under one rule and establishing a centralized administration.
 
• The Mauryan Empire was characterized by a highly organized bureaucracy and an efficient taxation system.
 
• Chandragupta was guided by his advisor **Chanakya (Kautilya)**, who authored the **Arthashastra**, a treatise on economics, politics, and governance.
 
 
 
• **Social Structure in Ancient India:**
 
 
• The Indian caste system, as described in later texts, was based on the division of society into four main **varnas**: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras.
 
• However, Megasthenes' account of seven classes highlights a functional division of labor rather than a rigid hereditary caste system.
 
• This distinction provides a unique perspective on the social dynamics during the Mauryan period.

questions.question: What is the rate of Health and Education Cess on Income Tax in the financial year 2020-21?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**0.04**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Health and Education Cess** is levied on the income tax payable by individuals, Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs), companies, and other taxpayers in India.
 
• The rate of Health and Education Cess for the financial year **2020-21** was **4%** of the income tax payable.
 
• It was introduced in the Union Budget **2018-19** to replace the earlier **Education Cess and Secondary & Higher Education Cess**.
 
• The cess is aimed at providing additional funds for promoting **health and education initiatives** across the country.
 
• This levy is calculated on the total amount of income tax (including surcharge, if any) and is mandatory for all taxpayers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Purpose of Health and Education Cess:**

 
 
• The primary objective is to generate additional revenue to fund key government schemes in the domains of **healthcare** and **education**.
 
• The funds collected are intended for improving the quality of healthcare services and ensuring quality education, particularly for the underprivileged.
 
 
 
• **Calculation of Health and Education Cess:**
 
 
• The cess is calculated as **4%** of the total tax liability, including any surcharge applicable on the income tax.
 
• For example, if the income tax payable is ₹10,000, the cess would be ₹400 (4% of ₹10,000).
 
 
 
• **Difference Between Cess and Surcharge:**
 
 
• A **cess** is levied for a specific purpose, and the revenue collected must be used only for that purpose. For example, Health and Education Cess is used only for health and education-related initiatives.
 
• A **surcharge**, on the other hand, is an additional charge on tax levied on high-income earners and is added to the government's general revenue.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• Before the introduction of the Health and Education Cess, there were two separate cesses: **Education Cess** (2%) and **Secondary & Higher Education Cess** (1%).
 
• In **2018**, these were merged into a single Health and Education Cess at a rate of **4%**.
 
 
 
• **Taxpayers Affected:**
 
 
• All categories of taxpayers, including individuals, Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs), firms, and companies, are subject to this cess.
 
• It is applicable regardless of the income slab or tax rate under which the taxpayer falls.

__
 
• The **Cauvery River** is one of the major rivers in southern India, flowing through the states of **Karnataka**, **Tamil Nadu**, **Kerala**, and the **Union Territory of Puducherry**.
 
• The **river basin** covers approximately **81,155 square kilometers**, with the majority of the area lying in **Karnataka and Tamil Nadu**.
 
• The **Cauvery River** originates from the **Brahmagiri hills in Kodagu district of Karnataka** and flows into the Bay of Bengal after traversing Tamil Nadu and a part of Kerala.
 
• **Andhra Pradesh** does not fall within the **Cauvery River basin**. The major rivers flowing through Andhra Pradesh include the **Krishna River**, **Godavari River**, and **Pennar River**.
 
• The inclusion of **Kerala** in the Cauvery basin is due to the presence of its tributaries like the **Bhavani River**, which originates in Kerala but primarily flows through Tamil Nadu.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cauvery River Overview:**

 
 
• The Cauvery River is referred to as the **"Ganga of the South"** due to its significance in irrigation, drinking water supply, and hydroelectric power generation.
 
• The river flows for a total length of approximately **805 km**, with a major portion of its journey traversing Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
 
• It forms a large delta in Tamil Nadu, which is one of the most fertile regions in India and is often referred to as the **"Rice Bowl of Tamil Nadu."**
 
 
 
• **Tributaries of Cauvery River:**
 
 
• Key tributaries of the Cauvery River include the **Hemavati, Harangi, Kabini, Bhavani, Noyyal, and Amaravati Rivers.**
 
• These tributaries originate in the Western Ghats and contribute significantly to the water flow of the Cauvery River.
 
 
 
• **Andhra Pradesh Rivers:**
 
 
• The major rivers flowing through Andhra Pradesh include:
 
 
• **Godavari River:** The second-longest river in India, originating from Maharashtra and flowing into Andhra Pradesh.
 
• **Krishna River:** Originates from the Western Ghats in Maharashtra and flows through Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh.
 
• **Pennar River:** A river flowing through southern Andhra Pradesh.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Water Disputes:**
 
 
• The **Cauvery Water Dispute** is one of the most contentious inter-state water disputes in India, primarily involving **Karnataka and Tamil Nadu**.
 
• The **Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (CWDT)** was constituted in **1990** to resolve the conflict, and the final award was given in **2007**.
 
• In **2018**, the **Supreme Court of India** modified the tribunal's decision, allocating more water to Karnataka while ensuring Tamil Nadu’s share.

questions.question: The Government of India Act, 1919, envisaged bicameral government for the first time in India under British rule. It fixed the term of the Council of State at ____ years.

__
 
• The **Government of India Act, 1919** was a significant constitutional reform introduced by the British government, also known as the **Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms**.
 
• The Act introduced the concept of a **bicameral legislature** for the first time in India under British rule, with two houses: the **Legislative Assembly** and the **Council of State**.
 
• The **Council of State** was the upper house of the legislature, and its members were elected and nominated.
 
• The **term for the Council of State** was fixed at **five years**, making it a notable provision under the Act.
 
• The Act also introduced the system of **dyarchy** in provincial administration, dividing subjects into "reserved" and "transferred" categories.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Government of India Act, 1919:**

 
 
• It was introduced to implement the recommendations of the **Montagu-Chelmsford Report**.
 
• The Act marked the beginning of constitutional reforms in India, preparing the groundwork for future developments like the Government of India Act, 1935.
 
• The Act aimed to increase the participation of Indians in governance while maintaining British control over critical areas.
 
 
 
• **Dyarchy System:**
 
 
• Under the Act, provincial subjects were divided into two categories: **Reserved** and **Transferred**.
 
• "Reserved" subjects were administered by the Governor and his Executive Council, while "Transferred" subjects were handled by Indian ministers.
 
• This system was introduced to gradually involve Indians in governance but retained British control over important areas like finance and law enforcement.
 
 
 
• **Bicameral Legislature:**
 
 
• The concept of a bicameral legislature introduced under this Act was new to Indian governance.
 
• The two houses were the **Legislative Assembly** (lower house) and the **Council of State** (upper house).
 
• Members of the Council of State were elected and nominated, with its term fixed at **five years**.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Act:**
 
 
• The reforms under the Act were criticized for being inadequate, but they laid the foundation for the eventual independence movement.
 
• It led to increased political awareness and participation among Indians, especially educated elites.
 
• The Act was later replaced by the **Government of India Act, 1935**, which introduced more comprehensive reforms.

• The address by the President is a constitutional requirement and marks the beginning of the parliamentary calendar.
 
• It serves as a platform where the President outlines the government's plans and policy priorities for the year ahead.
 
• This provision ensures that Parliament is updated on the government’s legislative and administrative agenda for the upcoming sessions.
 
• The practice of the President addressing both Houses is an important element of parliamentary democracy in India, reflecting the government's accountability to the legislature.

• **Significance of the President’s Address:**

questions.question: The small intestine is divided into duodenum, jejunum and __________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ileum**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **small intestine** is divided into three main parts: **duodenum, jejunum, and ileum**. These sections are vital for the digestion and absorption of nutrients.
 
• The **ileum** is the last and longest part of the small intestine. It connects the small intestine to the large intestine via the **ileocecal valve**.
 
• The ileum is specialized for the absorption of **vitamins, minerals, and nutrients**, especially **vitamin B12** and bile salts, which are crucial for maintaining metabolic processes.
 
• Unlike the jejunum and duodenum, the ileum has a higher density of **Peyer’s patches**, which are lymphoid tissues that play a role in immune function by monitoring intestinal bacteria.
 
• The ileum contains finger-like projections called **villi**, which enhance the surface area for nutrient absorption. These villi are covered by microvilli, further improving absorption efficiency.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Structure and Function of the Small Intestine:**

 
 
• The small intestine is approximately **6 meters long** and is divided into three parts: **duodenum, jejunum, and ileum.**
 
• The **duodenum** is the first section and is responsible for receiving partially digested food from the stomach and mixing it with bile and digestive enzymes.
 
• The **jejunum** is the middle section and is primarily involved in the absorption of sugars, amino acids, and fatty acids.
 
• The **ileum**, the final section, absorbs nutrients not absorbed by the jejunum, such as **vitamin B12 and bile salts**.
 
 
 
• **Large Intestine vs Small Intestine:**
 
 
• The **large intestine** is shorter (about 1.5 meters) and primarily absorbs water and salts while forming feces.
 
• The **small intestine** is longer and designed for nutrient absorption, with specialized structures like villi and microvilli.
 
• The small intestine connects to the large intestine via the **ileocecal valve**, ensuring the movement of digested food.
 
 
 
• **Digestive Functions of the Ileum:**
 
 
• The ileum absorbs **vitamins, fatty acids, and bile salts** essential for digestion.
 
• It contains specialized lymphoid tissues like **Peyer’s patches**, which help in immune surveillance.
 
• It is involved in recycling bile salts back to the liver, a process known as the **enterohepatic circulation**.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of the Small Intestine:**
 
 
• The small intestine has a large surface area due to the presence of **villi and microvilli**, facilitating efficient nutrient absorption.
 
• It is lined with enzymes that aid in breaking down carbohydrates, proteins, and fats into absorbable molecules.
 
• Its walls are rich in blood vessels, ensuring nutrients are transported into the bloodstream for distribution throughout the body.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Peyer’s patches:**

 
 
• These are specialized lymphoid tissues found in the ileum and play a critical role in the **immune system**.
 
• They monitor intestinal bacteria and prevent pathogenic bacteria from entering the bloodstream.
 
 
 
• **Ileocecal Valve:**
 
 
• This valve separates the ileum from the large intestine and prevents the backflow of contents into the small intestine.
 
• It ensures the proper movement of digested food for further processing in the large intestine.
 
 
 
• **Vitamin B12 Absorption:**
 
 
• The ileum absorbs **vitamin B12** bound to intrinsic factor, which is essential for **red blood cell formation** and neurological functions.

questions.question: What is the process of movement of gases in cells called?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Diffusion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Diffusion** is the process by which molecules, including gases, move from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration until equilibrium is achieved.
 
• This movement occurs due to the **random kinetic energy** of the molecules and does not require any external energy input.
 
• In cells, gases like **oxygen** and **carbon dioxide** diffuse across the cell membrane to facilitate processes such as **cellular respiration** and removal of waste products.
 
• Diffusion is a passive process, meaning it does not require energy from the cell. This makes it an efficient way of gas exchange in both plant and animal cells.
 
• The rate of diffusion depends on factors such as **temperature, concentration gradient, and the permeability of the membrane.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Pseudopodium:**

 
 
• A pseudopodium is a temporary, arm-like projection of a eukaryotic cell membrane.
 
• It is primarily involved in **cellular movement** or ingestion during processes like phagocytosis.
 
• While pseudopodia help in movement and feeding, they are not related to gas exchange.
 
 
 
• **Cytolysis:**
 
 
• Cytolysis refers to the bursting or breaking down of a cell when it takes in too much water.
 
• This occurs in a hypotonic solution and is not associated with the movement of gases.
 
 
 
• **Osmosis:**
 
 
• Osmosis is a type of diffusion but is specific to the movement of water molecules across a semipermeable membrane.
 
• It occurs from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration.
 
• Osmosis does not involve the movement of gases, making it different from the process in the question.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Diffusion:**
 
 
• Diffusion plays a critical role in **gas exchange** in both animals and plants.
 
• In humans, oxygen diffuses into the blood in the lungs, while carbon dioxide diffuses out.
 
• In plants, diffusion enables the exchange of gases during photosynthesis and respiration.
 
• It is essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis and supporting vital metabolic processes.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Gas exchange in animals:**

 
 
• In mammals, gas exchange occurs in the **alveoli** of the lungs via diffusion.
 
• Oxygen from inhaled air diffuses into the bloodstream, while carbon dioxide from the blood diffuses out into the air to be exhaled.
 
 
 
• **Gas exchange in plants:**
 
 
• Plants exchange gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide through small openings called **stomata**.
 
• Diffusion enables oxygen release and carbon dioxide intake during **photosynthesis**.
 
 
 
• **Applications of diffusion:**
 
 
• Diffusion is used in industries for separating gases, such as in gas purification systems.
 
• It is also a principle used in designing **artificial membranes** and medical devices like oxygen concentrators.

questions.question: According to the Union Budget 2020-21, which of the following was the largest source of finances for the Central Government during the financial year 2020-21?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Direct Taxes**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Direct Taxes** were the largest source of revenue for the Central Government in the Union Budget 2020-21. These include taxes like **Income Tax** and **Corporate Tax**, which are paid directly by individuals and corporations to the government.
 
• In the financial year 2020-21, **direct taxes accounted for approximately 56% of the total tax revenue**, highlighting their significance in the government’s revenue collection.
 
• **Income Tax** is levied on individuals, Hindu Undivided Families (HUF), and other non-corporate entities, while **Corporate Tax** is levied on the income of companies.
 
• Direct taxes are critical for funding government expenditures on infrastructure, welfare schemes, and public services, making them a cornerstone of fiscal policy.
 
• Other sources like **Central Excise**, **Custom Duty**, and **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** contribute to the revenue but are classified under indirect taxes, which are collected through intermediary businesses.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Direct Taxes:**

 
 
• Direct taxes are taxes paid directly to the government by the taxpayer, without any intermediary. Examples include **Income Tax** and **Corporate Tax**.
 
• They are progressive in nature, meaning the tax rate increases as the taxable amount increases, ensuring equity in tax collection.
 
• Direct taxes are a vital tool for reducing income disparities and funding public welfare projects.
 
• In the Union Budget 2020-21, direct taxes played a significant role in meeting government expenses, particularly during the pandemic-related economic downturn.
 
 
 
• **Central Excise:**
 
 
• This is an indirect tax levied on the manufacturing of goods within the country. It is collected from manufacturers and passed on to consumers.
 
• Post-GST implementation, excise duty is mainly applicable to petroleum products and alcohol for human consumption.
 
 
 
• **Custom Duty:**
 
 
• Custom duty is an indirect tax imposed on the import and export of goods. It is a significant source of revenue for the government.
 
• It helps protect domestic industries by making imported goods more expensive than locally manufactured goods.
 
 
 
• **Goods and Services Tax (GST):**
 
 
• GST is an indirect tax implemented in India on **1st July 2017** to subsume multiple indirect taxes like VAT, service tax, and excise duty.
 
• It is a multi-stage, destination-based tax applied on every value addition, simplifying the tax structure in the country.
 
• In the financial year 2020-21, GST contributed significantly to the government’s revenue, but its share was lower than that of direct taxes.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Union Budget 2020-21:**

 
 
• The budget estimated a total revenue of **₹20.20 lakh crore**, with a significant portion derived from taxes.
 
• Direct Taxes were the most substantial contributor, emphasizing their importance in government finances.
 
• The budget aimed to boost economic growth, improve infrastructure, and enhance welfare measures, especially in light of the economic challenges posed by COVID-19.
 
 
 
• **Tax-to-GDP Ratio:**
 
 
• The tax-to-GDP ratio is a critical indicator of a country’s fiscal health. For India, it was around **10.6%** in 2020-21.
 
• An increase in this ratio indicates improved tax compliance and effective revenue collection mechanisms.

• The budget was structured around three themes: **Aspirational India, Economic Development for All, and Caring Society.**
 
• Under the **'Economic Development for All'** theme, the government focused on boosting infrastructure, agriculture, and industrial growth.
 
 
 
• **Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas:**
 
 
• This slogan was first coined by **Prime Minister Narendra Modi** to emphasize the need for inclusive development.
 
• **'Sabka Saath'** implies collective efforts by all stakeholders, including the government, private sector, and the citizens.
 
• **'Sabka Vikas'** focuses on ensuring equitable development across all regions and communities.
 
• **'Sabka Vishwas'** underscores the importance of trust-building measures, especially with marginalized and underprivileged groups.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY):**

 
 
• Launched in **2015**, PMAY aims to achieve **Housing for All by 2022**.

• It provides a **subsidy on home loans** for economically weaker sections and low-income groups under the Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme (CLSS).
